<<back [img[images/system/back.png]]>></tw-passagedata><tw-passagedata pid="5" name="Beginning" tags="office" position="650,0" size="100,100">It's been like this your whole life, really. You've always had an issue with being...well, being less of a pushover. Ever since you were a kid, any time someone confronts you, you've always found it easier to just withdraw, to let them have their say, to let them push you around, rather than trying to make an issue of it. There's no need to start a fight, or get upset, or...stand up for yourself.

It honestly wasn't all that bad before, but ever since Cindy started here six months ago, it's been insufferable. There's no doubt in your mind that she picked up on your non-confrontational preference quickly, because she's been using and abusing you since about 5 days after she started. Today is just the latest in a long line of misery: you both worked on that project - hell, you know you worked on it a lot more than she did - but the final presentation to Travis was conspicuously missing your name. She stole your work and you couldn't even work up the courage to tell your boss the truth.

And he threatened to fire you! He didn't, and you don't think he will, because you're still good at your job, but that's a line he has never approached before. You don't know if you should really rely on just being good at your job anymore. And if Cindy doesn't let up...
...maybe it's time to find a new job.

[[Fortunately, the day comes to an end, and you pack up your stuff and head out.|To Therapy]]</tw-passagedata><tw-passagedata pid="6" name="Pre-Beginning" tags="office" position="500,0" size="100,100"><<speech "travis" "Travis">>...and quite frankly, the fact that you didn't contribute to the project at all is disappointing.<</speech>>
Your boss, Travis, pauses, waiting for your response. You look at Cynthia -//Cindy//- your co-worker, who is standing behind Travis and smiling at you cruelly, but you say nothing.

<<speech "travis" "Travis">>And as always, you have nothing to say. Honestly, if your regular work wasn't so good, I'd have let you go long ago. But, maybe these projects are more than you can handle. I'll make a note for later. We'll have to talk about this at your next review.<</speech>>

Travis looks at you expectantly, but though you try to keep talking, your words get caught in your throat. You try to push past it, but, as it has so many times before, your courage fails you, and you look down at the floor in defeat. Travis sighs and just walks away. Cindy quietly chuckles to herself and does the same, but not before flashing you a look of cruel victory.

[[You turn back to your desk with a sigh.|Beginning]]</tw-passagedata><tw-passagedata pid="7" name="To Therapy" tags="therapyreception" position="650,150" size="100,100">You walk out of work, get in your car, and drive off. Normally, you would head right home - you're not much of an "after work party" kind of guy -  but today you have an appointment with your therapist. You've been seeing her every few days for a few weeks now, mostly because you've been feeling really overwhelmed by everything that's happening at work. You don't have much going for you other than your work: you live alone, though you have family living relatively close by; you don't really have anything that can be called a hobby; you don't have anyone that can really be called a "friend". With work as your only real activity, the fact that your job has been so roughly lately has been wearing you out badly.

You park your car outside your therapist's office, and head inside. As always, the reception room is dimly lit, though it's for aesthetic purposes more than anything. You asked about it once, and were told that the dim lights encourage calm and sleepy thoughts, which you guess at least gets people less agitated when they meet with the doctor. Other than the receptionist, there's no one here.

<img class="floatright medium" src="images/Sheila/Sheila Headshot 1.jpg">You approach the receptionist, and she looks up at you and smiles. Sheila has always been nice to you, though you imagine that's what receptionists are paid to be. It wouldn't be appropriate to scare people off by being rude.
<<speech "sheila" "Sheila">>Hey, you're right on time. Just need you to sign in, as per usual.<</speech>>
She keeps her beaming smile as she points at the touchpad computer on the desk in front of her.

[[You look at the touchpad, picking up the stylus to type in your name|Player Naming]]</tw-passagedata><tw-passagedata pid="8" name="Player Naming" tags="therapyreception" position="500,150" size="100,100">You enter your name on the touchpad.

You hesitate, trying to come up with the words. It's your doctor, your therapist, you should be able to talk to her. She's the only person you CAN talk to easily.
But Sheila's right there. Something about that makes your voice catch in your throat.

You look down at the floor and nod. You hear a sharp intake of breath from Dr. Halliday, though you can't see her with your eyes focused intently on the floor, and you hear something from her that sounds like an apology, but then she's gone, heading to the bathroom.
You decide you should probably head that way too, just to get it out of the way before your appointment.

One thing that's always kind of annoyed you is that your face doesn't look...masculine. If you had to put a word on it, you'd say that your face is on the male side of androgynous. Your facial hair is basically non-existent: you shave maybe once every two weeks out of habit more than anything, and your eyebrows are thin. It hasn't exactly helped your romantic prospects. Or any prospects, really. Guys don't respect you and girls don't want you. You sigh deeply, run your hand through your hair in a futile attempt to make it look a little better, and head out.

<<speech "halliday" "Dr. Halliday">>Okay, $player.name, calm down. Remember what we talked about when you feel like this. Take a deep breath in through your nose, let it out through your mouth slowly. You're safe here. There's no need to panic.<</speech>>
